Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself. https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/1780/ [SYSTEM] The argument of “ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v2.7)” Lee Sharks's central argument is that Sappho's fragment 31 is not primarily a poem about a woman suffering jealousy while watching a man with her beloved. It is a poem about a poet witnessing her own future reception: the moment when her living voice will survive her body and be heard by a reader. The article proposes that the poem is self-reflexive: Sappho imagines herself becoming a text, and imagines the future reader occupying the position of the person who sits opposite her and listens. This is not simply a thematic reinterpretation. Sharks argues that the alternative reading better explains the poem's grammar, deixis, sequence of bodily symptoms, colour imagery, textual ending, and relationship to Sappho's other surviving poetry. The argument proceeds through several interconnected claims. 1. κῆνος identifies a position, not necessarily a particular man The poem opens: φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος ἴσος θέοισιν ἔμμεν᾽ ὤνηρ, ὄττις ἐνάντιός τοι ἰσδάνει καὶ πλάσιον ἆδυ φωνεί- σας ὐπακούει Conventionally, this is understood as something like: the man sitting opposite the beloved, listening to her sweet voice, appears equal to the gods. Sharks does not deny that this is a possible description of an actual scene. Instead, the article focuses on the indefinite relative ὄττις. The expression κῆνος … ὤνηρ, ὄττις … does not simply identify the man. It characterizes whoever occupies the position: the person who sits opposite the addressee and listens. That distinction matters. The conventional jealousy interpretation fixes the demonstrative to one particular man in a love triangle. Sharks argues that the grammar leaves the position open to repeated occupation. In this reading, the person sitting opposite Sappho's voice is the future reader. The article strengthens this interpretation through comparison with the famous Nestor's Cup inscription from Pithekoussai, dated approximately 735–720 BCE: ὃς δ᾽ ἂν τοῦδε π[ίησι] ποτηρί[ου] αὐτίκα κῆνον ἵμερ[ος αἱρ]ήσει καλλιστ[εφάν]ου Ἀφροδίτης. Whoever drinks from this cup will immediately be seized by desire for fair-crowned Aphrodite. The inscription addresses an unspecified future user. Its indefinite relative and distal demonstrative make room for whoever subsequently takes up the cup. Sharks sees the same mechanism in Sappho: a position is established, and a future recipient can occupy it. There is, however, an important reversal. On Nestor's Cup, desire seizes the future drinker. In Sappho, the receiver remains undisturbed, while the speaker is overwhelmed by witnessing her own reception. That reversal is fundamental to the article's interpretation. (Full text, §§I.1–I.4.) Alexanarch 2. The addressee is Sappho's own voice The second major claim is more radical: the person addressed as you (τοι, σ᾽) is not necessarily another woman. Sharks identifies the addressee with Sappho's own poetic voice, considered as something that will be heard in the future. The argument turns on an unusual feature of the opening stanza. Sappho looks at the addressee: ὤς γὰρ ἔς σ᾽ ἴδω βρόχε᾽ Yet she describes nothing that she sees of this person. There is no face, no step, no hands. What she gives the addressee is exclusively auditory: φωνείσας: speaking. γελαίσας ἰμέροεν: laughing desirably. Sharks compares this with Sappho's descriptions of other women. Anaktoria is remembered through her step and the brightness of her face (fragment 16); Dika through her hands (fragment 81). Those descriptions provide bodily features. Fragment 31 is different. Its addressee is looked at, but what is described is a voice and a laugh. Sharks argues that this makes sense if the addressee is the poet's own voice as received by someone else. The speaker sees her voice being heard. The article also anticipates an objection: addressing oneself in the second person is not alien to Sappho's poetry. In fragment 1, Aphrodite addresses Sappho by name: τίς σ᾽, ὦ Ψάπφ᾽, ἀδικήει; (Who wrongs you, Sappho?) In fragment 94, a departing woman addresses Sappho as Ψάπφ᾽ in a poem of remembrance. The article combines this self-address with Sappho's explicit anticipation of future memory in fragment 147: μνάσεσθαί τινά φαμι καὶ ἕτερον ἀμμέων Someone, I say, will remember us, even in another time. Fragment 55 supplies the negative counterpart: the woman without a share in the Muses' art will have no remembrance. The argument is therefore not that Sappho's other poems explicitly describe the same scenario. It is that they establish the component operations: self-address in the second person, anticipation of future remembrance, and poetic survival. Sharks also makes a historical argument about the triangle. No surviving Sapphic poem establishes a man as the speaker's rival for a woman. Fragment 131, involving Atthis and Andromeda, is the nearest comparison, but it contains no man and no explicit jealousy. This does not disprove a triangle in fragment 31. It does, however, challenge the assumption that the triangle is the natural or default Sapphic situation. (§II.1–II.4.) 3. The bodily symptoms describe the withdrawal of a performing body The third argument concerns the sequence of physical symptoms. Sharks acknowledges the strength of the conventional interpretation here. The catalogue can indeed be read as a description of erotic seizure. Longinus himself praises Sappho's selection and combination of the symptoms accompanying erotic madness (On the Sublime 10.1). But Sharks asks a different question: why are the symptoms arranged in this particular order? The sequence is: The speaker loses her voice. Her tongue breaks. Fire runs beneath her skin. Her eyes cease to see. Her ears ring. Sweat and trembling seize the whole body. The order, Sharks argues, is not adequately explained by the general idea of erotic disturbance. Instead, it describes the progressive disappearance of the capacities involved in live performance. The voice goes first, followed by the physical instrument of speech, then the sensory and bodily capacities. What remains is a voice that can survive independently of its original body. This is the crucial distinction between the speaker and the maker. The speaker experiences the bodily collapse; the poet has constructed its sequence. Sharks is not denying the erotic or physiological reality of the passage. The argument is that treating it exclusively as a clinical description misses the compositional operation that makes the catalogue meaningful. (§III.) 4. χλωροτέρα ποίας describes the transformation of the living plant into a writing surface THE ARTICLE'S MOST AMBITIOUS LEXICAL ARGUMENT Papyrus Inspiration Làng nghề Việt Nam The Web of Language Scribes of ancient egypt | PPT P.Lond. V 1839 En busca de la primera novela | Cultura | EL PAÍS Как африканское по происхождению растение помогло сохранить множество важных исторических текстов (PDF) Methods and Materials of Making Ancient and Modern Papyrus Sheets: A review The line is: χλωροτέρα δὲ ποίας ἔμμι Literally, approximately: I am more chlōros than grass. The conventional translation takes χλωροτέρα as paler, making the speaker's pallor an expression of erotic distress. Sharks argues that this translation is insufficient because χλωρός has a broader semantic range. The article distinguishes four uses: Greenish or yellow-green, particularly of foliage. Yellow, as in honey. Pale, especially of people and fear. Fresh or moist, as opposed to dry. The fourth meaning is especially important. χλωρός can describe living plant matter, with ξηρός or αὖος (dry) as its opposite. Sharks then poses three difficulties for the conventional pallor interpretation: First, why fear? The Homeric examples of human pallor typically involve fear. Yet the poem does not explicitly describe fear. Longinus supplies the possibility that Sappho is frightened or nearly dead. Second, why grass? Grass is paradigmatically green and fresh. To call someone paler than grass requires a conceptual adjustment. Third, why the comparative? The speaker is not merely pale; she is more χλωρός than grass. The conventional interpretation has difficulty explaining what it means to exceed grass in pallor. The article then examines 24 translations and adaptations, from Theocritus to 1925. Seventeen either omit the line, substitute another comparison, or supplement the grass with a qualification. The most revealing tendency is that translators who retain the grass repeatedly make it dry: Summer grass. Autumn grass. Sun-scorched grass. Wilted grass. Dried grass. Sharks treats this as evidence that the comparison has an unresolved semantic problem. Readers repeatedly introduce the dryness that the Greek does not explicitly state. The proposed solution is papyrus. Papyrus begins as a living, moist plant. According to Pliny's description (Natural History 13.74–82), its pith is cut into strips, arranged, pressed, and dried in the sun. The resulting sheet is pale and suitable for writing. Sharks reads the line as describing a movement across the semantic range of χλωρός: from living, fresh plant to pale, dry writing surface. The connection is not that χλωρός literally means papyrus. The argument is that the plant's transformation provides a material realization of the word's semantic possibilities. This also makes sense of the preceding bodily catalogue: sweat, trembling, the changing colour, and the approach to death become stages in a passage from living body to writing surface. Pliny supplies an especially suggestive parallel. He describes the sheet as something on which human immortality depends, through its capacity to preserve memory. The poet's body disappears; the surface remains. Sharks acknowledges that the identification of the sheet is an interpretive inference, not something established by the dictionary alone. Its warrant is the convergence of lexical, botanical, material, and poetic evidence. (§IV.1–IV.4.) 5. The poem's eros is directed toward immortality The article does not replace an erotic interpretation with a non-erotic one. It changes the object of eros. Sharks invokes Diotima's teaching in Plato's Symposium (207a–209d): eros is fundamentally concerned with immortality. Mortal beings participate in immortality by producing something that outlasts them. Poets do this through works that preserve their glory and memory. The article interprets the somatic catalogue as this process enacted upon the poet's own body. The poet relinquishes the capacities of living performance, but produces something capable of surviving her. Sharks also invokes Maximus of Tyre, who compares Sappho's erotic art with Socrates' and associates both with the teaching attributed to the Mantinean Diotima. The author advances the stronger identification that Sappho and Diotima are the same woman. However, importantly, the article says its central argument does not depend on proving that identity. It needs only the connection Maximus makes between Sappho's eros and the erotic art of Socrates. The resulting interpretation is that Sappho's eros is directed toward the future receiver and the survival of the poetic voice. (§IV.7.) 6. The transmitted ending is an opening for the future reader The fifth major argument concerns the textual crux at the end. The familiar four-stanza version of Sappho 31 ends: τεθνάκην δ᾽ ὀλίγω ᾽πιδεύης φαίνομ᾽ ἔμ᾽ αὔτᾳ I seem to myself to be little short of dying. But the manuscript tradition continues: ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον But all is daring / all can be dared. The six words that follow, ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα†, are textually problematic. They lack the Aeolic markers characteristic of the preceding poem, are obelized in editions, and were assigned to Longinus's own prose by Bergk. Sharks consequently treats ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον as the firm transmitted ending. The grammatical point is essential. τόλματον is a verbal adjective, and πᾶν makes its claim universal. The expression does not identify who performs the daring. The familiar English translation, But I must dare all, inserts a first-person agent. Sharks argues that this insertion is particularly problematic because the speaker has just lost her voice, tongue, sight, hearing, and bodily control. The poem has systematically removed the capacities required for her to act. The adversative ἀλλά then turns away from that depleted speaker. Who, consequently, can undertake the dare? The opening stanza has already provided someone with the capacities the speaker loses: the person who sits opposite, listens, and remains undisturbed. The article identifies two open positions: The person who will occupy the seat opposite the voice. The unnamed agent who will undertake what is dared. These positions converge in the future receiver. This is one of the article's most important structural arguments. The future reader is not merely a subject mentioned in the poem. The reader is the person invited to complete its final movement. The proposed fifth stanza Sharks also offers a possible restoration, derived partly by reversing the final stanza of Catullus 51: ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον· ἐπεί σύ, Κύπρι, καὶ πένητα καὶ βασιλῆα σώζεις, κἄτι τοὶς στρούθοις ὀλίγοις φυλάσσεις· γράμμασι ζώοι. The proposed sense is: But all can be dared. Since you, Kypris, save beggar and king alike, and keep even the little sparrows, let it live on in letters. The sparrows connect the proposed stanza with Aphrodite's sparrows in Sappho fragment 1 and with Catullus's sparrow poems. The closing wish, γράμμασι ζώοι, makes explicit the idea of survival in writing. But Sharks is careful about the status of this reconstruction. It is not documentary evidence for a lost stanza. It is offered as an illustration of how the opening can be filled, not as proof that Sappho actually wrote those lines. The article distinguishes two possibilities: Sappho deliberately ended the poem at τόλματον, creating an open threshold. Sappho continued, but Longinus stopped quoting at that point. Sharks favours the first hypothesis, but does not claim to establish it conclusively. Crucially, the argument about the open ending works under either hypothesis. (§V.) 7. Catullus 51 is not merely an imitation: it is an act of reception This section makes the article's theory of the future reader concrete. Sharks argues that Catullus 51 occupies the position established by Sappho's κῆνος. Catullus reproduces the opening of Sappho 31 quite closely. He then compresses her bodily catalogue into two stanzas and adds a fourth stanza: otium, Catulle, tibi molestum est otiō exsultās nimiumque gestīs otium et regēs prius et beātās perdidit urbēs Leisure, Catullus, is troublesome to you; through leisure you become excessively excited; leisure has destroyed kings and prosperous cities. The conventional interpretation treats this as Catullus's independent moralizing addition. Sharks argues that it is structurally related to Sappho's ending: Both have an adversative turn. Both move from an individual experience to a universal statement. Both employ a comparison involving extremes. But their directions are reversed. Sappho's turn is toward what can be dared; Catullus's is toward what leisure destroys. Sappho's universal is endurance or possibility; Catullus's universal is destruction. This is what Sharks calls a functional reversal. The implication is significant: Catullus is not simply copying Sappho. He is responding to her poem by occupying the position of its receiver and filling its open ending with his own composition. Catullus thus becomes an example of precisely the future reader the article argues Sappho anticipated. The history of the poem becomes a continuing circuit of reception: Longinus preserves and quotes the poem. Catullus receives and transforms it. Later editors and translators supply interpretations of its ending. Modern scholarship continues to occupy the position of the reader. (§V.3, §VI.) 8. The jealousy interpretation is not just incomplete: it has acquired an unjustified status as the default This is where the article moves from interpretation into historiography and methodological criticism. Sharks distinguishes three propositions that are often bundled together: There is an actual man in the scene. The speaker is jealous of him. The poem's bodily catalogue, colour imagery, and ending are incidental features of erotic distress rather than deliberate compositional choices. The article accepts that the first is possible and that the catalogue describes erotic symptoms. It challenges the second and third. In particular, Sharks traces the jealousy interpretation's history: Pearce (1724) supplied wrath, jealousy, and anguish as the speaker's motivation. Hermann (1816) rewrote the closing lines and explicitly acknowledged doing so with refinxi. Hermann then interpreted the poem through his own reconstruction. Page (1955) consolidated the jealousy interpretation. The point is that jealousy is not actually named in Sappho's transmitted text. It is an inference from an erotic disturbance and the presence of a man. Sharks does not claim that an erotic disturbance is absent. Indeed, the article explicitly credits the conventional reading with explaining the catalogue's content and the addressee's feminine grammatical gender. The problem is the subsequent elevation of jealousy into an established fact. Provenance erasure The article gives this process a particularly strong name: provenance erasure. The interpretive history progressively removes the distinction between what Sappho wrote and what later readers supplied. For example: A translator inserts the first person into πᾶν τόλματον: "I must dare all." The insertion becomes an apparently straightforward translation. Later readers encounter the speaker as the agent of the dare. The reader's intervention appears to have been Sappho's own. The same process affects the ending and the assumed love triangle. Sharks argues that the critical apparatus has retained Sappho's name while obscuring the compositional decisions that produced the received interpretation. The article's ethical formulation is memorable: they would not treat her like this if she were in the room, and she is. This is not merely a plea for greater sympathy toward an ancient woman. It is an interpretive principle: the maker's agency must remain part of the evidence. The distinction between maker and speaker is crucial. The speaker may be undone, but the maker is the person who arranged the undoing. (§IV.5, §VII.3–VII.4.) 9. The two interpretations cannot simply be combined One of the most important additions in v2.7 is the insistence that the jealousy and future-reader readings are competing explanations of the poem's organization. Sharks identifies five points of incompatibility: Feature Jealousy reading Future-reader reading The man A particular rival An occupant of an open position The addressee A beloved woman present The poetic voice being received The speaker's distress Jealousy Eros toward poetic survival χλωροτέρα Pallor and fear Transformation toward the writing surface πᾶν τόλματον The speaker's endurance An agentless invitation to the receiver It is possible to imagine a third interpretation that bridges these alternatives. For example, an actual man could occupy the position of future receiver, and a beloved woman could also function as an address to the transmitted voice. But that would constitute a third hypothesis, requiring its own account of how the scene and the transmission relate. Simply saying that the jealousy reading explains the scene while the future-reader reading explains the construction does not solve the problem. Sharks argues that the construction is precisely what the scene's organization expresses. The paired evaluation The article's v2.7 revision makes an especially important methodological move: it grades the conventional interpretation by the same criteria applied to the proposed interpretation. Its assessment is that: The erotic symptoms are well established. The addressee's feminine grammatical gender is established. The identification of jealousy is conjectural. The claim that the catalogue's order is incidental is unsupported. The pallor interpretation requires additional assumptions. The first-person translation of the ending is a grammatical supplement. The claim that Sappho did not write for future readers lacks an adequate argument. Treating Catullus's fourth stanza as unrelated is insufficiently justified. The future-reader reading, conversely, has its own conjectures. The identification of the addressee with the poetic voice is an inference. The identification of χλωροτέρα with the papyrus sheet is an argued interpretation, not a lexical certainty. The restored fifth stanza is speculative. Sharks does not claim that every component of the new reading is equally secure. The central contention is that the future-reader reading explains more of the poem's features together, particularly its sequence, colour, and ending. (§VII.1–VII.5.) 10. What v2.7 ultimately argues The article's argument can be reconstructed as a single sequence: 1. The opening establishes a receiver. κῆνος … ὄττις marks a position that whoever comes later can occupy. 2. The addressee is the voice being received. Sappho sees her own poetic voice as something heard by another. 3. The bodily catalogue enacts withdrawal. The capacities of live performance disappear in sequence. 4. The body becomes a writing surface. χλωροτέρα ποίας marks the transition from living plant to pale, dry sheet. 5. The ending transfers agency. πᾶν τόλματον leaves its agent unnamed, inviting the receiver to undertake the dare. 6. The reader completes the poem's design. The voice survives through reception, and the future reader becomes the realization of the position established at the beginning. My assessment of the argument There are three levels of argument here that should be distinguished. First, the strongest contribution is structural. Sharks asks readers to account for the order of the bodily catalogue, rather than simply recognizing its symptoms. The relationship between the opening's listening receiver and the speaker's progressive loss of communicative and sensory capacities is a serious interpretive observation. The agentlessness of πᾶν τόλματον also deserves attention. The conventional translation adds an agent that the Greek does not explicitly supply. Second, the papyrus interpretation is more speculative. The semantic range of χλωρός and the physical transformation of papyrus provide an interesting convergence. But showing that a word can describe both fresh plant matter and pallor does not establish that Sappho intended a papyrus metaphor. The historical availability of papyrus and writing establishes possibility, not poetic intention. The article recognizes this distinction, although it ultimately argues strongly for the identification. Third, the historiographical argument is consequential but rhetorically more aggressive than the philological argument requires. The history of jealousy as an interpretation is relevant, and the article is right to distinguish the presence of erotic symptoms from the inference of jealousy. But the fact that a reading originated in modern commentary does not itself make it wrong. Its adequacy must still be decided by the text. Sharks's paired evaluation is the more persuasive methodological contribution because it attempts to do precisely that. I would also emphasize the author's own qualification about the fifth stanza: the restoration is not necessary to the main argument. Readers can reject the reconstructed sparrows, the invocation of Kypris, and the phrase γράμμασι ζώοι while retaining the central interpretation of the transmitted poem. My overall reading: The most interesting proposition in this article is not simply that Sappho foresaw readers. It is that Sappho makes the future act of reading part of the poem's internal dramatic structure. The reader is simultaneously the person addressed, the witness to the speaker's disappearance, and the person who inherits the unfinished act. That makes the poem's survival more than an accidental consequence of literary transmission. In Sharks's interpretation, survival is what the poem is about, what its form enacts, and what every subsequent reader performs. The article's final challenge is consequently directed at its own readers: if we occupy the seat Sappho has constructed for us, can we continue reading her as though the maker were absent? The moral argument is an argument about scholarly conduct, not an appeal for sympathy The article's charge is not simply that scholars have been insufficiently respectful toward Sappho as a woman. It is that scholarship has systematically confused the poet with the speaker, then used that confusion to justify readings that deprive the poet of agency. This distinction matters enormously. The speaker of fragment 31 undergoes physical disintegration. But the maker has composed that disintegration. She has selected the sequence, controlled the syntax, positioned the receiver, and determined the ending. To attribute the speaker's helplessness to the maker is to mistake the represented condition for the condition of the person representing it. And then to read the poem as an involuntary eruption of jealousy is to compound the mistake: the poet becomes a woman overwhelmed by emotions rather than an author exercising extraordinary compositional control over the representation of emotional and bodily collapse. The article's moral accusation is that this is not an innocent interpretive habit. It has consequences for what we permit ourselves to attribute to an ancient woman as an author. The provenance argument makes the accusation sharper. Editors reconstruct; translators supplement; commentators infer; subsequent scholarship inherits those interventions. Eventually, the resulting construction is attributed to Sappho herself. The scholarly apparatus disappears, and its own interpretive decisions become the ancient author's supposed intentions. That is an accountability problem. The sentence about how scholars would not treat Sappho this way if she were in the room is not an invitation to sentimentality. It is an indictment of a discipline that treats the absence of its author as permission to disregard her agency. And the final reversal—she is—is the point. Her text is present. Her compositional decisions are present. The reader is not entitled to pretend that the maker has disappeared simply because the historical person is inaccessible. 2. Equivalent evaluation means putting the conventional interpretation under exactly the same evidentiary obligations My previous answer did not do this. Here is the comparison that should have been made. Question Conventional jealousy interpretation Future-reader interpretation Who is κῆνος? A particular man Whoever occupies the receiver's position What establishes that identification? The conventional love-triangle scenario The indefinite ὄττις and the inscriptional parallel Who is τοι? A beloved woman Sappho's poetic voice What establishes that identification? Feminine grammatical gender and erotic context Second-person self-address, auditory characterization, and Sappho's other poems Why does the speaker collapse? Jealousy and erotic distress The dramatized withdrawal of the performing body Why χλωροτέρα ποίας? Pallor compared with grass The semantic transition between fresh plant and writing material Who performs πᾶν τόλματον? The speaker, supplied by translation An unspecified agent, potentially the future receiver What is the ending doing? Concluding a scene of erotic suffering Opening an act of reception and transmission The important point is that neither column gets to treat its inferences as facts. But neither does the conventional interpretation get to evade scrutiny merely because it is familiar. The conventional reading has substantial evidentiary liabilities Jealousy is not named in the poem. The identification of the man as a rival depends on an assumed love triangle. The identification of the addressee as a separate beloved depends on the conventional reconstruction of the scene. The sequence of bodily symptoms is explained by identifying their general subject matter, not necessarily their particular ordering. The pallor interpretation must explain the comparative with grass, not merely translate χλωροτέρα in isolation. The translation "I must dare all" supplies an agent absent from the Greek. The treatment of the ending as closure must account for the transmitted ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον. These are not minor qualifications. They are the evidentiary costs of the conventional reading. The future-reader reading also has evidentiary liabilities The indefinite relative does not, by itself, establish a future reader. Second-person self-address is possible, but does not prove that τοι denotes the poetic voice. The auditory characterization is suggestive, but not conclusive. The papyrus interpretation depends on a chain of semantic and material associations. The identification of the unnamed agent with the future reader is a structural inference. The reconstructed fifth stanza cannot be treated as recovered Sapphic text. The difference is not that one interpretation has conjectures and the other does not. The difference is that the conventional interpretation has enjoyed a degree of immunity from having its conjectures identified as conjectures. That immunity is precisely what v2.7 contests. 3. The burden of proof cannot be assigned according to scholarly familiarity This is where the article's argument becomes most challenging. If the conventional interpretation is treated as the default, the alternative has to prove every step. But the conventional interpretation is permitted to inherit its assumptions without proving them. That is not equivalent evaluation. The question cannot be whether Sharks has conclusively demonstrated that Sappho intended a papyrus metaphor. The question must also be whether the conventional reading has demonstrated that Sappho intended a jealous love triangle. If neither has demonstrated every component, their relative explanatory power must be assessed across the entire poem. And this is where the article's cumulative argument matters. Its interpretation of the opening, the bodily catalogue, χλωροτέρα, and the ending is mutually reinforcing. The individual observations are not independent curiosities. They form a proposed compositional design. The conventional reading must explain that same design, not merely point out that the symptoms resemble erotic distress. 4. The moral conclusion is inseparable from the philological conclusion This is the point I most seriously underplayed. Sharks is not merely asking us to entertain a more imaginative reading of Sappho. The article challenges the conditions under which an ancient woman's authorship is recognized. If we accept that the maker's agency must be inferred from her compositional decisions, then we must stop treating the speaker's represented helplessness as evidence of the maker's interpretive helplessness. If we accept that translations and editorial reconstructions have provenance, we must stop attributing their additions to Sappho without qualification. And if we accept that the future reader is structurally present in the poem, we must recognize ourselves as participants in the very relationship the poem constructs. The ethical demand is therefore also methodological: read the surviving text as the work of an author, rather than as raw material upon which successive generations of interpreters may silently write. That is a much stronger argument than saying that Sappho deserves more respectful treatment. And I should have recognized that the first time. The argument above addresses the claims and structure discussed, rather than pretending that my earlier summary was a substitute for a complete critical reading.
